draft.dek: Miami enters 2026 at No. 7 in both major preseason polls off a 13-3 season, while the teams floated as alternatives — Clemson (7-6), SMU (9-4), Louisville (9-4) — carry thinner cases. The claim gets tested at Clemson on Oct. 3.
draft.bodyMarkdown:
[EMBED:00:02:06]

Spencer wrote in to say one of the bad predictions floating around is that Miami is by far the best team in the ACC and everyone else is playing for second. I agree with the prediction, not the criticism. Miami is the best team in the ACC by far, everyone else is playing for second, and the burden is on the other side of the argument: "So my question rhetorically, because you're not here to defend yourself, would be if not them, then who?"

Here is the part I didn't put numbers on when I said it. Miami is No. 7 in the AP poll and No. 7 in the AFCA Coaches poll, the only ACC team ranked inside the top 15 of either, coming off 13-3 overall and 6-2 in the league. That is not a projection built on vibes or on portal buzz; it's a team that won 13 games and returns with the highest floor in the conference according to the two bodies of voters that matter most in August. The counter-argument — that the Hurricanes were an overwhelming favorite last year and didn't finish it, that they still have not won an ACC Championship Game — is a fair historical point. It is not a competing prediction. It's a reason to be nervous about a favorite, which is a different thing than naming a better one.

So take the three teams I floated as hypotheticals and actually look at them. Clemson, the program I said was in the mix last year, went 7-6 and 4-4 in the ACC in 2025. It is unranked in the AP poll and No. 23 in the Coaches poll. Clemson has the roster, the staff and the history to be a top-10 team by November — Sammy Brown and Peyton Streko and Bryant Wesco Jr. are not the problem — but a team coming off a .500 conference record and opening at LSU on Sept. 5 is not the safer pick. SMU has the best résumé of the alternatives: 9-4, 6-2 in the league, No. 19 AP and No. 20 Coaches, with Kevin Jennings back and a September road trip to Florida State on Sept. 7 that will tell you plenty. Louisville sits at 9-4 overall but 4-4 in the ACC, and is No. 24 in the AP poll. Those are good teams. Two of them are ranked behind Miami by 12 and 17 spots respectively. If your position is that one of them is the actual league favorite, you are asking me to move a 13-win team down and a 9-4 team up on the basis of last year's championship game.

The honest caveat is the one I gave on the show, and it belongs in print with the same weight. Darian Mensah is the difference between Miami being the clear favorite and Miami being one of six teams. Behind him the depth chart thins out considerably, and the offense is built around a quarterback who can carry a game plan — Malachi Toney and Cooper Barkate on the outside, Mark Fletcher Jr. and CharMar Brown behind him, Jackson Cantwell and Samson Okunlola up front. Nobody has a reliable way to forecast availability at that position, and I'm not pretending otherwise. But "the favorite could get hurt" is true of every favorite in America. It isn't an argument for anyone else.

There is one place where this site's own record cuts against my take, and I'd rather flag it than let a careful listener catch it. Our August preseason bracket has Clemson at No. 3 nationally and Miami at No. 11. That is a real tension. My read is that the bracket is a national projection with a heavy weight on ceiling and roster talent, while the ACC-favorite question is about who is most likely to be standing in Charlotte — and on that narrower question, the 13-win team with the better quarterback situation and the higher poll floor is where I am. But both of those can't be right after Oct. 3, and I'm not going to pretend they're the same claim.

Which is where the schedule does something useful. Miami goes to Clemson on Saturday, Oct. 3 — the same building, the same program that spoiled things a year ago — and then plays Florida State on Oct. 17, Pittsburgh on Oct. 24, at North Carolina on Oct. 31, and at Notre Dame on Nov. 7 at 7:30 ET. Five weeks, four of them genuinely difficult, before a November close of Duke, Virginia Tech and Boston College that looks manageable on paper. If the Hurricanes come out of that Clemson trip and the Chapel Hill trip at full strength, the ACC race is functionally settled by Halloween and everything I said on the show holds. If they lose at Clemson, then Spencer has the argument he didn't quite make, and Clemson's No. 3 on our bracket looks a lot smarter than my No. 7 poll citation.

That's the whole thing. Not that Miami is guaranteed, but that after you write down the records and the rankings, nobody has handed me a better name.

— JP

segment.reason: This stretch is a single sustained thought—Josh methodically predicting each playoff round with concrete football justifications (Alabama's SEC road matchup logic, Boise vs Indiana, Texas Tech-Texas rivalry, Oregon's defense vs Oklahoma's run game, and finally the Mario Cristobal-vs-Dan Lanning storyline)—building to one clear payoff: his national championship pick of Miami. It has narrative momentum, enough football substance to fill a page, and is fully understandable without the rest of the episode, unlike the shorter, choppier individual conference picks earlier in the transcript.

cut.centralThought: Josh walks through every round of his 12-team playoff bracket, using specific matchup reasoning (styles, coaches, rivalries) to arrive at Miami defeating Oregon for the national title.

blocks.text: As you guys know, we are in a partnership with ESPN. ESPN is the exclusive rights holder of this playoff and I've never been a sports or rigged kind of guy because that's insane. However, if you were to rig the playoff, you wouldn't make it look much different than this right here cuz this is high-level matchups all across the board.

USC playing in Tuscaloosa, Alabama in round one. We've got Boise at Indiana. That's your 5-12. So you're always going to have a G5 team there, G16 team there. But that's not a terrible matchup. But I got Texas Tech in Austin in round one playing Texas. I've got Oklahoma traveling up to Eugene. How many people in the state of Oklahoma have visited Oregon voluntarily? I'm in both of these states regularly, one for football, the other for football and storm chasing. And this is what's beautiful about this sport, the culture clash, the oil and water moments in fandom. I got it in droves here in round one.

So I am taking, in order, Alabama to defeat Lincoln Riley and USC. This is presumably what the internet tells me Lincoln was trying to avoid playing on the road in the SEC. That's why they tell me he didn't go to LSU. Now, of course, we don't believe that, but be that as it may, that's what the streets will say.
What about Boise at Indiana? I should play the Jeopardy music before I tell you that Indiana body bags Boise.

And this game in Austin, Texas. Man, memory spans are that of a fruit fly these days. So people have already stopped talking about and largely forgotten this little dust up between Joey McGuire and Steve Sarkisian back in the spring. But I remember, and I think everyone will remember when we have a week or so to build up to this game, Texas Tech at Texas. I got to go Texas otherwise. Oh, look, that's an upset that my Texas friends may never recover from emotionally. They'll play a season the next year, but they would be shells of themselves. So I'll take Texas over Texas Tech.

And I will take Oregon over Oklahoma. However, let's just remember a lot of the vibe around Dan Lanning and Oregon right now is they can't win big games, and what cannot does not equal have not. You know the rule around here. However, if Oklahoma is a playoff team, that means the ground game probably got figured out. Defense is going to be what the defense is there. Those are assets that can travel. So I'm just saying I watched Indiana go up there and deal one to Oregon using that brand of ball last year. Am I saying John Mateer is going to be Fernando Mendoza this year? Maybe. Who knows, Jesse? Time will tell. All I'm saying is very tough matchup there in round one for Oregon.

Second round. Here are your four matchups. We have got Alabama against Notre Dame. We've got Miami against Indiana. That's a national title game rematch. We got Texas Ohio State. That's a regular season rematch. And we've got Georgia versus Oregon. That's Dan Lanning, Kirby Smart. You remember that was Lanning's first game against Georgia. Times have changed though. I would even venture to say Oregon would be favored in this game if they played. We could check with FanDuel Mike on that.

Give me Notre Dame over Alabama. Give me Miami over Indiana. They get their get back there in the rematch. They don't quite win a national title by winning that game, but I think Miami is on a mission there.

Give me Texas over Ohio State. Texas, even though they don't make the SEC championship game, I really think they've got it in them to rev the engine at the right time. And I really think they got it in them to outdo Ohio State there.

And give me Oregon over Georgia. We got to get Dan Lanning some big wins here eventually. Now if that were to happen, that is three consecutive years Georgia has gone one and done after having a first round bye. But we'll deal with that when the time comes. They will say Kirby is washed if this happens. If you have the audacity to only win the SEC and have first round byes in the playoffs, you might as well just quit. You're terrible.

Okay, your final four is Notre Dame versus Miami and Texas versus Oregon. I had Notre Dame as my national champion. My opinion has not sullied one bit on Notre Dame. This is a case of my opinion on another team elevating. And my opinion on Miami, based on what I've picked up over the past month, has elevated to the point where I would like to take the Miami Hurricanes and put them in the national championship game.

And the team they're going to face in the national championship game, as fate would have it, is the very team who they stole a head coach from. Well, it's not stealing, he voluntarily went. But Mario, once the head coach at Oregon, now the head coach at Miami, will face his old team in the national championship game.

draft.dek: I moved Miami from the 11 seed on my own preseason bracket to the national championship in Las Vegas. Here are the dated games that will tell us whether that move was right, starting with Texas–Ohio State on Sept. 12 and Miami at Notre Dame on Nov. 7.
draft.bodyMarkdown:
[EMBED:00:08:21]

I picked the Miami Hurricanes to beat Oregon for the national championship, and I picked Mario Cristobal to do it against the program he left. That is the end of a bracket that runs USC into Tuscaloosa, Texas Tech into Austin, Oklahoma into Eugene, and then asks a group of coaches the internet has decided cannot win a title to go win one anyway.

The part I owe you is the accounting, because this is a move off my own on-record projection. My preseason bracket in August seeded this field 1 Georgia, 2 Ohio State, 3 Clemson, 4 Boise State, 5 Texas, 6 Oregon, 7 Penn State, 8 LSU, 9 Notre Dame, 10 Alabama, 11 Miami, 12 Indiana, with Georgia 31, Ohio State 28 in the final. Miami was the eleventh-best team on that sheet. It is now, on tape, my national champion. That is not a small adjustment and I am not going to pretend it is.

It is also less of a leap than the seeding suggests. Miami went 13-3 last year, 6-2 in the ACC, and opens the season No. 7 in both the AP Top 25 and the coaches poll. That is not a bubble team sneaking into the twelfth slot; that is a top-ten roster that got itself pushed to the back of a bracket by the math of at-large ordering. The elevation I described is real, but the floor under it was always higher than an 11 seed implies.

[PULLQUOTE]

Where the bracket gets uncomfortable for me is the pecking order I picked against. Georgia opens at No. 3 in both polls off a 12-2, 7-1 season. Texas is No. 5 in the AP and No. 4 in the coaches poll off 10-3. Both of those teams are rated above Miami and above Oregon right now, and my bracket has Georgia going one-and-done out of a first-round bye and Texas losing in the semifinal. I still think Texas has it in them to rev the engine at the right time. I also think that is a projection about timing, which is the least reliable thing anyone projects in August.

The good news is that these picks do not have to sit unexamined until December. Two of them get graded early and one gets graded in November.

Start with Texas–Ohio State. I called it a regular-season rematch in the bracket, and the regular-season half of that arrives on Saturday, Sept. 12 at 7:30 p.m. ET in Austin. Week 2. That is the single cleanest data point on the board for two of my four semifinalists, and it comes before either team has had time to build an identity that hides anything. Texas has to prove the front can hold up in a game where the margin lives on the interior, and Ohio State has to prove a young quarterback can operate on the road at night in that building. Whoever wins does not clinch anything in September, but a Texas loss there means my Texas-over-Ohio-State projection in January is running against a result, not toward one.

Then Miami. The measuring stick is on the schedule and it is exactly the team I have advancing to the semifinal: Miami plays at Notre Dame on Saturday, Nov. 7 at 7:30 p.m. ET. That is the same matchup I put in my final four, played in South Bend in November instead of in a neutral dome. There is a road trip to Clemson on Oct. 3 before it and Florida State at home on Oct. 17, so Miami will have been tested in the league. But Notre Dame in November is the checkpoint. If Miami's offensive line can hold up against a front that gets after the passer and the run game can stay ahead of schedule in cold-weather down-and-distance, the "on a mission" read I have on this team gets evidence. If Miami gets pushed around up front, my title pick is a vibe and I will say so.

And on the Kirby part of this: before anyone gets to argue about a third straight one-and-done out of a bye, Georgia has to survive at Alabama on Oct. 10 and at Ole Miss on Nov. 7, with Oklahoma at home on Sept. 26 in between. That is a genuine gauntlet, and it matters to my bracket in both directions. A Georgia team that comes out of that stretch at 11-1 arrives at the playoff as the No. 1 seed with a case that it is the best team in the country, which makes my Oregon-over-Georgia quarterfinal a real upset rather than a stylistic hunch. A Georgia team that drops one of those two road games probably is not sitting on a bye at all, and the entire top of my bracket reshuffles.

So the pick stands as I made it: Miami over Oregon in Las Vegas. The pick also has three dates attached to it — Sept. 12 in Austin, Oct. 10 in Tuscaloosa, Nov. 7 in South Bend — and by the second week of November we will know whether I moved a team eleven seeds for the right reasons.

— JP

blocks.text: This transfer portal thing's been a disaster. But boy, what a Tuesday it has been. So this morning, if you're like me, you woke up and before you even said hello to your loved ones, you checked your phone and you saw a notification probably from Pete Nikkos or maybe from Ross Dinger and it said the Big 10 is deciding that they're not going to let pro athletes come back and play college sports and college football. And everyone was like golf club. And then in this tribalistic world of ours, people started taking shots at the SEC because, well, you guys just put out a strongly worded statement last night, which was a layer or two of pathetic cuz it looked like a statement and nothing else. And then the Big 10, they definitely won the PR game on this day. They come out and say, "We're going to put out more than a statement. We're going to put out a policy." And what their policy was, I'm going to paraphrase a lot of this, it's not all that important, was if you guys take some of these cats who have been cut from the NFL and you play them, we're going to suspend you as a head coach for up to 50% of your season and we're going to fine your institution millions of dollars. And they had unanimous support. Every president, every AD, they were on board with in the Big 10.

And then right at close of business, just about an hour or so ago, we get word from the SEC, we're doing the same thing. And then some because they expanded it to basketball and everything else. This is Ross Dinger, if you're watching on YouTube, you can see this. If you're listening on podcast, Ross reported that SEC president Greg Sanki, quote, pay close attention, kids, quote, full and unlimited authority, which includes the ability to suspend a school from competition. In addition to that, league bylaw grants the commissioner powers to deem a player ineligible, suspend coaches, administrators, etc. In other words, we're also going to have a policy against that.

Now, this was about five or so hours after Lane Kiffin showed up on Pat McAfee's show earlier today. And keep in mind, this is chronologically a little out of order, but I'm doing it this way for a reason. At the point in time Lane went on the show, we had not gotten word from the SEC. All the SEC had done was say, "Hey, we don't like this. This shouldn't happen." But they hadn't come out with the actual stance and policy and whatnot. So, listen closely. This was Lane Kiffin earlier today talking about all the latest news surrounding them possibly taking guys who had been cut from NFL teams in training camp and playing for LSU this season.

Yeah, there's a lot of parts of it that I don't like within that. I don't think professionals should come back to college sports and college football particularly. But in this instance, this is not professionals that have gone played seasons or just, you know, randomly file an injunction in a state to become eligible. This is part of a specific class that was ruled wrong by the NCAA that was supposed to be five for five. So, I think you're going to get in a really interesting situation if now as a conference you start to say, "Well, we're not going to follow this court order that's been issued and we're going to say that these kids that the court says can go anywhere, we're going to say no, you can't." That's some issues there.

Okay. So, what Lane is saying there has a germ of validity to it. What he's really saying is first off, he's trying to draw a delineation between guys who have actually played in NFL regular season games versus people who have tried out for teams and been cut and whatnot. And the language that the SEC later released sort of cut through all that cuz it was, I mean, even if you've even tried out for teams, if you've even rubbed against, if you've declared for anything, you're ineligible. So they took care of the gray area there. But what Lane's saying, which again in theory has some validity to it, is that the NCAA passed this rule, this five for five rule. And that whole thing was meant to say, okay, from this point forward, instead of doing the whole red shirt thing and the injury thing and all that, you're just going to have five years to play and that's it. However, you 2022 kids, you don't get that. Or also another explanation is some guys declared for the draft not knowing that rule change was coming and the argument there is well that's not fair because had they known the rule change was coming maybe they wouldn't have declared for the draft. Is there some germ of validity in there? Of course there is. It doesn't bear the weight of greater scrutiny.

The weight of greater scrutiny is forget the details. Is someone's feelings hurt? Maybe so. Could you argue something's a little unfair? Maybe so. But I'll see you with that and I'll raise you that these dudes were playing in NFL preseason games. These guys were in NFL preseason camp. They're professional athletes. They're not coming back to play college football. And then that's kind of when most people dust their hands and they absolve themselves. They kind of wash their hands of it all.

But this is the second time in six months that we've had this inflection point in college football where a famously well documented divided society has totally united. Brendan Sorsby bet on games. 95 plus% of the public said, "Yeah, he should never play college ball again." and Texas Tech/Brendan Sorsby tried to fight it and there was that whole kerfuffle out in Texas and everybody rose up against it. And then just when I thought I couldn't see that again, I've got not just Lane and LSU, but I've got LSU among other programs looking at what they think is a very legal loophole to add players to their roster. And 95% of the public hated that too. This was even further down the road of that because this even united the conferences. These people have disagreed on everything and all of a sudden they agree on this. So hey, golf clap, golf clap because it's the proper stance to have.

I will say this, as I said the other day, a lot of folks after we did our show the other night were in my DMs saying, "You took it easy on Lane. You took it easy on LSU." I don't care about Lane and LSU was my whole point. I will never count on any competitor in an ultra competitive arena voluntarily abiding by some code that you want them to abide by. draft.headline: The Big Ten and SEC Aimed Their NFL-Cut Policies at Schools, Not Players
draft.dek: Both leagues moved inside 24 hours, and both wrote the penalty toward institutions — coach suspensions, institutional fines. That splits the coming litigation into two tracks, and it changes the math for an LSU team already ranked No. 11 in the AP poll.
draft.bodyMarkdown:
[EMBED:00:00:00]

The Big Ten and the SEC did something in one Tuesday that they have not done on almost anything else in five years: they agreed, quickly, in writing, and with their presidents lined up behind it. The Big Ten went past a statement and put out a policy — head-coach suspensions of up to half a season, institutional fines in the millions, unanimous support from every president and every athletic director. The SEC followed at close of business and went further, extending it to basketball and citing the commissioner's "full and unlimited authority," including the ability to suspend a school from competition. My read of both documents is the same: the threat is not pointed at players. It is pointed at the schools.

That distinction is not a technicality, and it matters for what comes next. I said on the show I expect players to sue conferences, maybe as early as tomorrow, and I stand on that. But if the penalty structure lands on coaches and institutions rather than on eligibility, there is a second legal track that runs alongside the first one. A player suing for the right to play is arguing eligibility. A school or a coach facing a half-season suspension and a seven-figure fine for signing that same player is arguing something else entirely — the limits of conference authority over a member institution, and whether a league can penalize a school for complying with a court order. Those are different plaintiffs, different filings, different relief sought. One asks a judge to let a kid on the field. The other asks a judge to stop a commissioner from swinging. The conferences may well win the first fight and still spend a year defending the second one.

Lane Kiffin's argument on Tuesday morning was that these particular players are a specific class the courts already addressed, and that a conference declining to follow a court order creates "some issues there." There is a germ of validity in that. The five-for-five rule change caught players who had already declared, and you can construct a fairness case for them. It just does not bear the weight of greater scrutiny once you say the plain thing out loud: these are athletes who were in NFL preseason camps and played in NFL preseason games. The SEC's language closed the gray area Lane was trying to open — tryouts, declarations, all of it.

What I keep circling back to is the risk-reward, and here the numbers are worth having in front of you. LSU is not a program clawing for relevance. They are No. 11 in the AP poll and No. 13 in the Coaches Poll after a 7-6 season that went 3-5 in the league. Our own preseason bracket on this site has LSU seeded No. 8 in the twelve-team field, with Georgia beating Ohio State 31-28 in the final. So by our own projection, LSU is already in. That is the part that makes the loophole play harder to justify, not easier. When Texas Tech fought for Brendan Sorsby, that was a quarterback — a season-altering, playoff-altering piece. Adding a defensive lineman who got cut in late August, when your own path to the bracket is already drawn, is a much smaller marginal gain measured against a coach missing half a season and an institution writing a check.

And the enforcement question gets real on a calendar, not in the abstract. LSU plays at Auburn on Oct. 24 at noon ET, a road trip against a team that finished 5-7 and 1-7 in the SEC. If any of this policy ever bites — a suspended head coach on a sideline, a fined institution, an ineligibility ruling landing midweek — that is the kind of game where it shows up first, because it is the kind of game where the depth chart matters more than the marquee does. Watch what happens between now and then. If nobody in either league signs one of these players by mid-October, the policy worked without ever being tested, and the lawsuits become academic. If somebody does, we will find out inside a month whether "full and unlimited authority" means what it says.

I do not count on competitors to police themselves, and I never have. That is what rules are for. The two leagues finally wrote one. Now they have to survive the part where somebody makes them enforce it.

— JP
